newsitem.title: UK: Australian group says it can cut coal pollution.
newsitem.headline: Australian group says it can cut coal pollution.

text.p: A newly-developed coal combustion catalyst may slash the emission of pollutants from coal burning, a main cause of acid rain, while boosting thermal output at the same time, its developer claims.

Coal Corp, a private Australia-based company which develops environmental protection products, said tests on its catalyst Sulph-X show cuts of up to 89 percent in sulphur dioxide emissions when mixed with coal before burning.
Coal Corp said industry experts said the results, if economically viable, could be significant to industrialised nations, where sulphur dioxide and other emissions cause acid rain.

The company cited a report by the U.K.-based Coal Research Establishment (CRE) which recently conducted tests on Sulph-X, which said the sulphur particles are captured in the slag and can be used safely as aggregate.

The company said in a statement that the mean SO2 concentration of the flue gases of the lignite, a young coal, alone was 142 milligrams per cubic metre but with Sulph-X added it fell to 15 mg/cubic metre.
"This represents an 89 percent reduction in sulphur dioxide emissions," Coal Corp said.
Coal Corp said Sulph-X also raises thermal output by five to 25 percent.
And at an average cost of treating one tonne of coal at $1.10, a weight additive of 0.38 percent, it is cheap.
However, some coal industry experts said the economics of the process would depend on the disposal of the remaining ash and on the type of plants that can use the catalyst.
"The type of area where it might be applicable seems to be small plants, it is unlikely to be economical on bigger plants," said one, who declined to be named.
"There may be something in it for a particular application but I don't think it will save the world."

Coal Corp managing director, Gordon Subloo who bought the rights to the techonology in China in the 1990s and has developped it since, said some 15 plants, mainly small power stations, use Sulph-X there.
But now, he is eyeing a wider market.
"The economic and ecological implications of Sulph-X could be very significant," Subloo said.
He said power stations need "scrubbers" that cost some 400 million stg ($668.8 million) to maintain flues by countering the extreme damage from the sulphur.
"In the U.K., which now imports 50 percent of its coal from the U.S., there are abundant stocks of high sulphur content coal which could be used if the catalyst was employed," he added.

In 1996, U.K. power stations used 54 million metric tonnes of coal, he said. When Sulph-X is added, and energy output increased by 20 percent, approximately 10 million metric tonnes less coal is needed, he added.

Subloo said Sulph-X, which can be sprayed on the coal prior to combustion or dissolved into water before the solution is spread onto the coal, leaves a sulphuric ash that can be neutralised using a lime bath.
But experts said that the tests seem to have concentrated on lignite, a young coal, and results on other coal types differing in ash content are not known.
Subloo said that further testing will be done, adding he expected the results would be more or less uniform.
The experts also voiced concern about the leftover ash from the use of Sulph-X, which Coal Corp says is made up of oxidisers, additives and desulpharisers. No tests have been done yet on the ash.
"We don't know what these substances really are, they could be harmful," one said.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
